subject: economics
topicDisplay: Theme 1 Introduction To Markets And Market Failure
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An outward shift of the entire PPF is most likely caused by:
options: A movement from inside to a point on the curve
A reallocation of resources between the two goods
An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
questions.explain: Economic growth shifting the PPF outward requires more or better resources or improved technology.

questions.q: The statutory incidence of an indirect tax falls on the producer, but the burden passed to consumers is greatest when demand is:
questions.explain: When demand is inelastic consumers keep buying, so firms can pass on most of the tax through higher prices.

questions.q: A negative cross elasticity of demand (XED) between two goods indicates they are:
questions.explain: Complements have negative XED because a rise in one good's price reduces demand for the jointly consumed good.

questions.q: Two goods with a positive cross elasticity of demand (XED) are:
questions.explain: A positive XED means a rise in one good's price raises demand for the other, indicating substitutes.

questions.q: A negative production externality exists when:
options: Marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost
Marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit
Marginal private benefit equals marginal social benefit
Marginal private cost exceeds marginal social cost
questions.explain: A negative production externality means the cost to society (MSC) is greater than the private cost borne by the firm (MPC), creating a divergence equal to the external cost.

questions.q: Non-rivalry in consumption means that:
options: One person's consumption reduces the amount available to others
People can be excluded from consuming the good
One person's consumption does not diminish the amount available to others
questions.explain: Non-rivalry means the good can be consumed by additional people at no extra cost and without reducing others' consumption.

questions.q: A 'nudge' in behavioural economics is a policy that:
options: Alters the choice architecture to influence behaviour without removing options
Imposes a large tax to change behaviour
questions.explain: Nudges change the way choices are presented to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice.

questions.q: A point inside (below) the production possibility frontier indicates:
options: Inefficient use of resources or unemployment
Productively efficient use of all resources
questions.explain: Points inside the PPF show resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, so output could rise with no opportunity cost.

questions.q: A normal good that is a luxury has a YED that is:
questions.explain: Luxuries are income elastic with YED greater than one, so demand rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.q: Information asymmetry in a market refers to a situation where:
options: The government withholds information from firms
One party in a transaction has more or better information than the other
Prices fully reflect all available information
questions.explain: Information asymmetry occurs when one party (e.g. the seller) holds more relevant information than the other, leading to misallocation of resources.

questions.q: Moral hazard arises when:
options: A party changes its behaviour after a transaction because it no longer bears full risk
Buyers and sellers have identical information
questions.explain: Moral hazard occurs post-contract when one party takes greater risks because the costs fall on another party, a result of asymmetric information.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers of a good with positive externalities shifts the:
options: Supply curve to the left, raising price
Supply curve to the right, lowering price and increasing output toward the social optimum
questions.explain: A producer subsidy lowers costs, shifting supply right so output rises toward the optimum where MSB equals MSC.

questions.q: A specific (per-unit) indirect tax shifts the supply curve:
options: Vertically upwards by a constant amount
Vertically upwards by a larger amount at higher prices
questions.explain: A specific tax adds a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply up by the same vertical distance at every quantity.

questions.q: A behavioural 'nudge' is a form of intervention that:
options: Alters the choice architecture to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice
questions.explain: Nudges change the way choices are presented (e.g. default options) to influence decisions without removing options or using price.

questions.q: If supply is perfectly elastic, the supply curve is:
questions.explain: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal because firms supply any quantity at a single given price.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when intervention:
options: Increases consumer surplus without any cost
Results in a net welfare loss or a misallocation of resources
questions.explain: Government failure arises when state intervention causes a more inefficient allocation of resources than would have existed otherwise.

questions.q: The deadweight welfare loss from a negative production externality is the area:
options: Above the supply curve at zero output
Between MSC and MPC, between the free-market and socially optimal outputs
questions.explain: The welfare loss triangle lies between the MSC and MPC curves over the range of over-production beyond the social optimum.

questions.q: A demerit good such as tobacco is characterised by:
options: Marginal social benefit exceeding marginal private benefit
Marginal private benefit exceeding marginal social benefit, causing over-consumption
questions.explain: Demerit goods are over-consumed because consumers overvalue the private benefit and ignore the external costs imposed on society.

questions.q: Making automatic pension enrolment the default option exploits which behavioural insight?
questions.explain: Default options exploit inertia, as people tend to stick with the pre-set choice rather than opt out.

questions.q: A positive consumption externality means that, at the free-market equilibrium, society:
options: Under-consumes the good relative to the social optimum
questions.explain: When MSB exceeds MPB, the market under-consumes because consumers ignore the external benefits, justifying a subsidy.

questions.q: A good with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
questions.explain: A coefficient between 0 and -1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.q: Producer surplus is the area:
options: Below the demand curve and above price
Below the supply curve and below price
Above the supply curve and below the market price
questions.explain: Producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum price firms would accept, shown above the supply curve.

questions.q: Regulatory capture is an example of government failure in which:
options: Regulators act in the public interest at all times
A regulator comes to serve the interests of the firms it is supposed to regulate
questions.explain: Regulatory capture occurs when the regulating body is dominated by the industry's interests rather than protecting consumers.

questions.q: An indirect tax used to correct a negative externality should ideally be set equal to:
options: The marginal external cost at the socially optimal output
questions.explain: A Pigouvian tax internalises the externality by being set equal to the marginal external cost at the social optimum, aligning MPC with MSC.

questions.q: 'Anchoring' as a behavioural bias means that consumers:
options: Rely too heavily on an initial reference value when making decisions
questions.explain: Anchoring describes over-reliance on a first piece of information, such as an original price, when judging value.

questions.q: The price elasticity of demand (PED) is calculated as:
options: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price
% change in quantity demanded / % change in income
% change in price / % change in quantity demanded
Change in quantity / change in price
questions.explain: PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, so quantity is divided by price.

questions.q: Which statement is a normative economic statement?
options: A 1% rise in price reduced quantity demanded by 2%
The government ought to raise the minimum wage
Unemployment fell by 50,000 over the year
questions.explain: Normative statements involve value judgements about what ought to be, rather than testable facts.

questions.q: At the midpoint of a straight-line, downward-sloping demand curve, PED is:
questions.explain: Along a straight-line demand curve, the midpoint has unit elasticity where total revenue is maximised.

questions.q: A necessity good with few substitutes typically has demand that is:
questions.explain: Necessities with few substitutes have inelastic demand because consumers continue buying despite price changes.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is best described as:
options: The total revenue earned by firms
The amount firms receive above marginal cost
The difference between the price paid and the maximum consumers were willing to pay
The deadweight loss from a tax
questions.explain: Consumer surplus is the gap between the maximum a consumer would pay and the price actually paid.
